analysis.one_liner: Raises federal employee pay 4.7% plus 4% locality pay for 2024.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise federal workers' pay by 8.7% in 2024 was referred to a Senate committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised pay for the roughly two million federal civilian workers in 2024: a 4.7% increase in base pay for salaried employees and for hourly wage-grade workers, plus a 4% boost in locality pay that varies by region, for a combined 8.7% raise [S2] [S3]. It was introduced by Senator Brian Schatz with 15 original cosponsors and picked up 20 total, all Democrats or the independent Senator Sanders [S1] [S4]. It was sent to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee and no further action was ever taken [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Federal civilian employees: salaried workers under the statutory pay systems (the General Schedule) and prevailing-rate employees, the hourly blue-collar federal workers such as mechanics and maintenance staff whose pay is normally set by local wage surveys [S2] [S3]. An 8.7% raise would have been roughly double the size of the annual federal pay adjustments of recent years, with the locality component worth more to workers in high-cost regions.

how_it_helps.text: Raises basic pay by 4.7% in calendar year 2024 for employees under the statutory pay systems, the salaried white-collar federal workforce.
Also raises pay by 4.7% for prevailing rate employees, the hourly wage-grade federal workers normally paid from local wage surveys, overriding that survey process for the year.
Adds a separate 4% locality pay increase on top of the base adjustment, for a combined 8.7% raise under the bill's title.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through larger agency payroll budgets. The bill text contains no offset or spending cut to cover the cost [S3].

drawbacks.text: The raise is an across-the-board percentage increase with no targeting: higher-paid senior officials and executives get the same 8.7% as a frontline wage-grade worker, and the biggest dollar gains go to the highest salaries.
The bill provides no funding source or offset, so the added payroll cost falls entirely on federal budgets and taxpayers.

The benefit is concentrated on about two million federal employees rather than the workforce at large, at a time when many private-sector workers had no comparable guaranteed raise, which is the standard good-faith objection to large federal pay bills.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers covered, this was a substantial raise, and the inclusion of wage-grade hourly workers meant the lowest-paid federal employees were not left out. The honest costs are real: the bill was not paid for, the percentage formula delivers the most dollars to the highest earners, and the beneficiary pool is narrow. Whether an 8.7% raise was the right size is a fair argument, but the bill never got far enough for that argument to happen.

outcome.mechanism: It went to the Senate Homeland Security committee the day it was introduced and sat there for the rest of the Congress, with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Senator Schatz introduced the bill on January 26, 2023 with 15 original cosponsors, all Democrats plus Senator Sanders.
The bill was read twice and referred the same day to the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.
Twenty senators cosponsored the bill in total: 19 of the 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of the 4 independents. No Republican cosponsored.
The action history shows no further action of any kind through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal pay budgets and the taxpayers who fund them are better off, since the unbudgeted 8.7% raise never happened. The roughly two million federal workers the bill covered are worse off: they did not receive the increase, and the bill was never debated or voted on, so the public record contains no explanation of why the committee let it die.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal pay budgets; the raise never happened

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.role: U.S. Senator from Hawaii; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise federal pay 8.7% in 2024 and recruited 15 original cosponsors.

against.name: Sen. Gary Peters
against.role: Chair, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Committee took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing or markup was ever held in the two years it sat there.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote at any point in the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 cosponsors were Democrats or the independent Senator Sanders; no Republican signed on, and the Democratic-run committee that held the bill took no action on it.

industries.industry: Federal employee unions and the federal workforce
industries.note: A raise of this size would have gone directly to unionized and non-union federal workers alike, with the wage-grade hourly workers included alongside salaried staff. The bill's death means this interest gained nothing from it; no industry loses or profits from the bill either way, since the cost is spread across taxpayers.
